title: Lemonade Change
description: Brute force to optimized: a general change search versus two simple counters ($5, $10) with a greedy preference rule.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: At a lemonade stand, each lemonade costs $5. Customers pay with a $5, $10, or $20 bill, one at a time, and must receive exact change for the amount over $5. You start with no change on hand. Determine if you can provide correct change to every customer, in the order they arrive.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Provide exact change using only bills received so far\"","Since only $5 and $10 bills are ever usable AS change, track just those two counts"],["A $20 bill can never be given back as change for anything","It never needs to be tracked at all, only $5 and $10 counts matter"]]}

blocks.text: Since lemonade costs $5, a $5 bill needs no change, a $10 bill needs $5 change, and a $20 bill needs $15 change (either three $5 bills, or one $10 plus one $5). Because $20 bills are never usable as change themselves, only the running counts of $5 and $10 bills received matter, no need to track anything more complex.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Cash Register with Only Two Useful Coin Types
blocks.text: Picture a cash register where only two denominations of change are ever handed back to customers; a large bill received is simply banked and never given as change itself. Tracking just how many of each USEFUL denomination you currently have on hand is all that is needed to know whether the next customer can be given correct change.

blocks.caption: Only $5 and $10 bills are ever given as change; two simple counters capture everything needed

blocks.text: Result: true. Three $5 bills received first (no change needed), then a $10 (give one $5 as change), then a $20 (give the remaining $5 plus the $10 as change).

Before tracking every bill ever received in a general structure, notice that $20 bills are NEVER given back as change, so only the counts of $5 and $10 bills currently on hand matter, letting two simple counters fully capture the state needed.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A $5 bill requires no change, so it simply increments the count of $5 bills on hand.

Observation 2: A $10 bill requires $5 in change, so it needs at least one $5 bill available; if so, use one $5 bill and gain one $10 bill.

Observation 3: A $20 bill requires $15 in change, preferably given as one $10 bill plus one $5 bill (preserving more $5 bills, which are more broadly useful for future change); if no $10 bill is available, three $5 bills must be used instead.

Observation 4: Preferring the $10-plus-$5 combination over three $5 bills whenever possible is the greedy choice, since $5 bills are strictly more valuable to keep on hand (usable for BOTH future $10 and $20 changes, while $10 bills are only useful for $20 changes).
This leads to maintaining two counters (five, ten); for each bill, apply the appropriate change rule, preferring to use a $10 bill (if available) over three $5 bills when making change for a $20.
Track every bill received in a general multiset (or list), and for each new bill requiring change, search for a valid combination of bills currently on hand summing to the needed change amount.

items: Maintain a list (or multiset) of all bills currently on hand.
For a $10 bill, search the list for a $5 bill to use as change.
For a $20 bill, search the list for a valid combination summing to $15 (checking combinations rather than using a direct rule).

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Tracking a general list and searching for valid change combinations directly handles the problem without assuming which denominations matter.
This does unnecessary work, since $20 bills are provably never useful as change, and the search itself is more complex than needed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) per bill in the worst case (due to sorting the on-hand list repeatedly), O(n squared log n) overall.
Space: O(n) for the on-hand list.
Limitation: recognizing that only $5 and $10 counts ever matter (since $20 bills are never given as change) reduces this to two simple counters and O(1) work per bill.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why general tracking is unnecessary: a $20 bill received is NEVER given back as change to any future customer, so it never needs to be tracked at all beyond the moment it is received.

The two-counter simplification: only the counts of $5 and $10 bills currently on hand ever matter, reducing the entire state to two integers.

The greedy change rule for $20 bills: prefer using a $10 bill plus a $5 bill (if available) over three $5 bills, since $5 bills are more broadly useful (needed for BOTH $10 and $20 change), so preserving them is strictly better.

The core idea: two counters, updated with simple O(1) rules per bill, replace any general search entirely.

Maintain five and ten counters. For a $5 bill, increment five. For a $10 bill, require five > 0, decrement five, increment ten. For a $20 bill, prefer ten > 0 and five > 0 (decrement both); otherwise require five >= 3 (decrement by 3); otherwise fail.

blocks.caption: Two counters and simple O(1) rules per bill fully solve the problem

blocks.text: Since a $20 bill is never given back as change, tracking it is unnecessary the moment it is received; only the counts of $5 and $10 bills on hand ever influence future ability to make change. Preferring one $10 plus one $5 over three $5 bills when change for a $20 is possible either way is provably optimal: it conserves $5 bills, which are strictly more flexible (usable for both future $10 and $20 change), so this greedy preference never leaves the solver worse off than any alternative choice.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with O(1) work per bill.
Space: O(1) extra.

blocks.text: Lemonade Change demonstrates recognizing that only a SUBSET of possible state (here, just $5 and $10 counts, never $20) actually matters, collapsing what could look like a general search problem into simple counters and O(1) rules.

items: Preferring three $5 bills over one $10 plus one $5 when both are possible, wasting $5 bills that could be needed later.
Forgetting that a $20 bill itself is never usable as change and does not need to be tracked at all.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["The very first customer pays with a $10 or $20","No change is available yet, correctly returns false."],["All customers pay with exactly $5","Always succeeds trivially, since no change is ever needed."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "a $20 bill is never given as change, so only $5 and $10 counts matter" simplifies the entire problem and should be the very first observation stated.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "provide change using only bills received so far", think: identify which denominations are ever actually reusable as change, and track only those.

items: How would this change if lemonade could cost a different, non-round amount?
How would you adapt this if bills could also be denominations like $1 or $2?
Any "greedy resource management with a preference for preserving more flexible resources" problem.
Coin Change style problems, though this one is simpler due to the very limited set of relevant denominations.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: A general change-search approach costs far more than necessary; the two-counter greedy approach runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: track only the state that actually matters (here, $5 and $10 counts), applying simple greedy rules per input.
Core Idea: for a $20 bill, prefer using a $10 plus a $5 over three $5s, since $5 bills are more broadly useful to preserve.
Time: O(n squared log n) for a general change search, O(n) for the two-counter approach.
Most Important Observation: a $20 bill is never itself usable as change, so it never needs to be tracked.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible greedy problem rewarding recognizing which state actually matters.
One line memory trick: track only $5 and $10 counts; prefer $10+$5 over three $5s for $20 change.
